title: Are the Pillars of Creation Already Gone?
description: The iconic Pillars of Creation span four light-years across the Eagle Nebula. But infrared observations suggest a supernova blast may have already wiped them out.

beats.text: The four-light-year Pillars of Creation may have already been completely destroyed.
beats.visual: Hubble visible-light image of the Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula, 1995

beats.text: Hubble captured these towers in 1995, revealing embryonic stars forming inside dense hydrogen pockets called EGGs.
beats.visual: Hubble Space Telescope Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 photo of the Eagle Nebula, 1995

beats.text: Nearby massive stars blast intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds across the gas.
beats.visual: Wide-field view of massive young stars eroding gas in the Eagle Nebula, 2014

beats.text: This photoevaporation slowly strips the gas away from each developing protostar.
beats.visual: Close-up Hubble image of evaporating gaseous globules in the Eagle Nebula, 1995

beats.text: When an EGG is uncovered, its forming star abruptly stops growing.
beats.visual: Hubble detailed view of an exposed star-forming globule tip, 2014

beats.text: Spitzer observations suggest a supernova shockwave wiped out the pillars 6,000 years ago.
beats.visual: Spitzer Space Telescope infrared image showing heated dust around the Pillars of Creation, 2007

beats.text: Astronomer Stephen Reynolds disputed the blast, arguing stellar winds heat the dust and erode it gradually.
beats.visual: High-resolution visible revisit of the Pillars of Creation taken by Hubble, 2014

beats.text: Because the nebula sits 7,000 light-years away, telescopes must wait 1,000 years to see if we are still watching them.
beats.visual: James Webb Space Telescope NIRCam infrared view of the Pillars of Creation, 2022
